newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU farm ministers to attack planned cereal aid cut.
newsitem.headline: EU farm ministers to attack planned cereal aid cut.

text.p: European Union farm ministers are expected next week to renew an attack on proposals to cut subsidies to cereals and oilseed farmers by 1.4 billion Ecus to aid beef producers hit by the mad cow crisis, diplomats said.

At a two-day meeting starting in Luxembourg on Monday, ministers will also receive a progress report on negotiations with the United States on meat imports and discuss options to reform olive oil subsidies so as to curb massive fraud.
Ministers are likely to argue that new budgetary forecasts show that sharp arable farming aid cuts will be unnecessary mainly due to a firmer dollar and a decline in the cost of export subsidies.
"Ministers will want to get things off their chests," said a Dutch EU presidency official.

The cereals and oilseed aid cuts were attached to an otherwise straightforward 1997/98 (July/June) farm price package of mostly unchanged prices proposed last month by EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler.
Ministers are expected to press for sweeteners for their farmers but no decisions are expected until after the European Parliament has given its opinion in June.
Fischler is likely to stand firm and will brief ministers on new reports on cereals, beef and dairy market trends into the next century which officials say may reinforce the case for more reforms.

Under the current proposal for 1.4 billion Ecus of subsidy cuts, cereals and oilseeds area aid would be cut by 7.3 percent and 4.2 percent respectively while set-aside payments would be slashed by 27 percent.
Most member states are also resisting proposals to cut cereals and sugar storage aid to take account of lower costs resulting from a fall in interest rates.
Fischler is seeking a nine percent cut to 1.0 Ecus a tonne in the monthly increase in payments for cereals held in intervention stores.
He has also sought to cut the monthly sugar storage refund by 17 percent to 0.35 Ecus per 100 kg.
Officials said farm ministers would not change the European Commission's negotiating mandate ahead of a resumption of meat trade talks with the U.S. in Washington next week.
"Ninety percent has already been agreed. There's only poultry left," the Dutch official said, referring to a dispute over poultry carcass decontamination methods.
On April 1, the EU imposed new poultry inspection rules blocking shipments worth an estimated $50 million annually.
This week, Washington delayed retaliatory measures on some $300 million of imports of EU meat until April 30 in the hope that agreement could be reached by then.
On olive oil, Spain is expected to lead producer countries in fiercely attacking Commission plans to link subsidy payments on the number of productive trees.
Spain, which says tens of thousands of people would be thrown out of work, wants to simplify the existing aid regime based on production and consumption.
"Both options remain on the table," a Commission spokesman stressed, adding Fischler would visit producer countries.
